newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan commemorates Kobe earthquake anniversary.
newsitem.headline: Japan commemorates Kobe earthquake anniversary.

text.p: Early morning commuters prayed silently on trains and 6,425 candles were lit for victims as residents of this port city on Friday marked the second anniversary of the devastating Kobe earthquake.

Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto and most members of his cabinet travelled to Kobe for commemorative ceremonies held against a backdrop of criticism of inadequate government efforts to help the poorest victims of Japan's worst natural disaster for 70 years.

The earthquake, measuring 7.2 on the Richter scale, killed more than 6,425 people, injured nearly 40,000, and damaged or destroyed more than 400,000 homes when it shook the city to its foundations at 5.46 a.m. on January 17, 1995.
City officials say nearly 70,000 people are still either in temporary housing or living with relatives after surviving what is officially called the Great Hanshin Earthquake.
"Most of them lead lives of uncertainity with poor prospects of finding new homes or jobs," the Yomiuri Shimbun newspaper said in an editorial.
"It is vital that help be extended to those having trouble in reestablishing themselves, but there have been no words of reassurance from the government in this regard," it added.
Under a scheme to help people who cannot afford to rebuild their old homes or move elsewhere, new government-funded homes are allocated by regularly held lotteries as they are built.
But the pace of building has not kept up with demand and some homeless, mainly the elderly, cannot afford the cost of maintaining a home even if they win in the lottery.

Many homeless were present at the day's first and most moving ceremony, a dawn vigil in a park where candles were lit for each of the 6,425 dead and arranged on the ground to represent a map of the world.
"Last year, the candles marked out a map of Japan. This year we wanted the world to know of our sadness and suffering," a vigil organiser said.

Hideko Onishi, 74, told Reuters that after living through Japan's three great 20th century tragedies -- the 1923 Tokyo earthquake, which killed more than 100,000 people, World War Two and the Kobe disaster --- it was always the elderly who suffered the most.
"Sadness becomes deeper with time," she said. "And it's always the same. The elderly are the ones who get forgotten and suffer the most."
Many homeless are elderly people without resources or prospects to earn money that would allow them to start their lives again.

Tamotsu Miyamoto, 59, burst into tears when he said he had not been able to sleep in the 24 hours before the anniversary because of memories of a sister who died in fires which swept the city after the tremor.
"It becomes more difficult to cope with grief and living, the longer life goes on," he said.
Seiichi Kinoshita, 52, said his life had become a tragedy since the earthquake.
"My older brother died on the day of the quake. Then my mother died a few weeks later from grief. Then my father died last year from the hardship of rebuilding our lives," he said.
